extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers, graduate students), mathematical community interested in research quality
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the multiple dimensions by which mathematical work may be judged (e.g. problem-solving, technique, exposition, depth, applicability), including consideration of field context and long-term generativity; illustrated by the Szemerédi theorem case study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a major breakthrough on an important mathematical problem
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values results that solve central, pressing problems. Example: breakthroughs resolving long-standing conjectures. Score higher when the problem is widely recognised as important and the solution opens further avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a masterful use of existing methods, or the development of new tools
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses originality and power of methods introduced or applied. Includes creation of tools that others can reuse. Note: technical sophistication is valuable when it clarifies or simplifies subsequent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical theory
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a conceptual framework or choice of notation which systematically unifies and generalises an existing body of results
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewards unifying frameworks that organise disparate results. Consider scope of unification, clarity of concepts, and ability to predict or guide future results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical insight
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a major conceptual simplification, or the realisation of a unifying principle, heuristic, analogy, or theme
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looks for conceptual leaps that change how problems are viewed. Insight often precedes formal development; value clear heuristics and analogies that lead to rigorous work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. the revelation of an unexpected and intriguing new mathematical phenomenon, connection, or counterexample
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewards discoveries that reveal new phenomena or counterexamples that reshape feasible approaches. Examples include Behrend's construction and other illuminating examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical application
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. to important problems in physics, engineering, computer science, statistics, etc., or from one field of mathematics to another
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values applicability and cross-fertilisation. Assess how effectively mathematics is translated to other domains or used to solve practical/theoretical problems in different areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a detailed and informative survey on a timely mathematical topic, or a clear and well-motivated argument
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses clarity, pedagogical value, and accessibility. Good exposition can broaden impact of results and attract new researchers; rewarded by surveys, expository articles, and lucid lecture notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a lecture or writing style which enables others to learn and do mathematics more effectively, or contributions to mathematical education
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values teaching ability, clarity of presentation for learners, and creation of educational resources. Important for cultivating future talent and disseminating knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical vision
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a long-range and fruitful program or set of conjectures
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses leadership in setting research agendas, proposing conjectures and programs that motivate sustained research. Consider influence on community direction and generation of follow-up work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical taste
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a research goal which is inherently interesting and impacts important topics, themes, or questions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates choice of problems and goals: whether they are inherently compelling and likely to matter. Taste is partly subjective and culturally influenced; high taste often correlates with lasting relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. an effective showcasing of a mathematical achievement to non-mathematicians, or from one field of mathematics to another
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looks at exposition for broader audiences, communication of significance, and translation of results across fields. Enhances visibility and support for mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good meta-mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. advances in the foundations, philosophy, history, scholarship, or practice of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes foundational work, historical scholarship, and analyses of practice. Value contributions that clarify the nature, limits, or methods of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: with all details correctly and carefully given in full
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses correctness, completeness of proofs, and attention to detail. The text notes rigour is crucial but is only one component of quality; balance rigour with other virtues depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. the amazing identities of Ramanujan; results which are easy (and pretty) to state but not to prove
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewards aesthetic appeal: simplicity of statement, surprising connections, and elegance. Beauty is subjective but often signals conceptual clarity and wide interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegant mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. Paul Erdős’ concept of 'proofs from the Book'; achieving a difficult result with a minimum of effort
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values concise, clever proofs and minimal machinery. Elegant proofs often illuminate deeper structure and are highly prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a radically new and original technique, viewpoint, or species of result
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses originality and novelty of approach. Creative work expands the toolkit and can open new subfields; consider risk and potential payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a lemma or method which will be used repeatedly in future work on the subject
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures practical utility and frequency of reuse. Tools and lemmas that become standard are especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a sharp result that matches the known counterexamples, or a result which deduces an unexpectedly strong conclusion from a seemingly weak hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates sharpness and optimality. Strong results push limits; check whether bounds are optimal or close to known obstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a result which is manifestly non-trivial, for instance by capturing a subtle phenomenon beyond the reach of more elementary tools
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses conceptual depth and the need for sophisticated structure. Deep results often require new theories and have long-term significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitive mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. an argument which is natural and easily visualisable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values intuition and accessibility of ideas. Intuitive arguments help build understanding and pedagogy; they may precede formalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitive mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: e.g. a classification of all objects of a certain type; the final word on a mathematical topic
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewards completeness and finality: classification theorems and closure of problems. Such results settle questions decisively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance across multiple qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical quality is high-dimensional and different qualities (e.g. rigour, creativity, exposition) may trade off; a healthy field values plural approaches
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-emphasising one dimension at the expense of others. Evaluate whether a field or work is overly narrow (ornate baroque generalisation, conjecture proliferation without progress, ad hoc problem solving without unifying theme, overly dry technical formalism, or reverence for classical results without new contributions). The page gives five hypothetical anti-patterns illustrating unhealthy imbalances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical alignment with state of the field
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as 'good' depends on the state of a field (mature fields may need theory-building; emerging fields may benefit from conjectures and experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fitness of approach to current needs: are resources best spent on systematic programs, new conjectures, conceptual simplification, publicity/introductions, or other aims? Context-sensitive weighting of criteria is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community consensus and continual updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Fields should maintain at least a partial (but evolving) consensus within each field as to which qualities to prize most
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages ongoing debate about priorities; consensus helps allocate scarce resources (money, time, attention, talent, journal space) efficiently. Also suggests specialisation of recognition (prizes/journals) to cover multiple dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generativity / ability to produce further mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematics tends to beget more good mathematics in many other senses, generating further results, methods, and directions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a piece initiates a larger mathematical story, spawns new techniques, enables broad applications, or catalyses subsequent breakthroughs (e.g. Szemerédi’s theorem leading to regularity lemma, ergodic theory connections, transference to primes). This 'generativity' is a high-value trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitting into a greater mathematical story (global context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good mathematics is often part of a greater story that unfolds to generate many further pieces of mathematics of different types
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a result connects with previous work and its potential to be integrated into larger programs. Potential to be 'a piece of a larger puzzle' increases long-term importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent approaches and robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Different proofs/approaches (combinatorial, ergodic, Fourier-analytic, hypergraph) strengthen understanding and indicate deep structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value when a result admits diverse methods: this suggests robustness and multiple lines of further development. The Szemerédi case study highlights four distinct approaches leading to cross-fertilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative strength and bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of quantitative bounds and effective estimates (e.g. better bounds for van der Waerden or Szemerédi-type results)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess improvements in explicit constants, rates, and quantitative effectiveness. Consider whether better bounds unlock applications or expose limitations (e.g. Gowers' and Shelah's improvements and Gowers' lower bounds on regularity lemma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness despite incomplete or heuristic arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematics need not be absolutely correct in every detail to be of value to future rigorous work
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges heuristics, non-rigorous analogies, or preliminary constructions can be influential (e.g. interim constructions in prime gaps). Evaluate influence, plausibility, and whether later work can make heuristics rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of structure vs randomness dichotomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many methods and results exploit a dichotomy between structure (algebraic models, characteristic factors) and randomness (mixing properties, pseudorandomness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work articulates or exploits a useful structure/randomness dichotomy and whether it isolates the correct notion of pseudorandomness/uniformity for the problem at hand (as in Gowers' uniformity norms, Host-Kra cube averages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns indicating unhealthy focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of unhealthy field behaviours: excessive ornamentation/generalisation without direction; many conjectures without path to proof; ad hoc unrelated problem solving; excessive technical recasting without breakthroughs; reverence for classical results without producing new ones
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these scenarios as negative diagnostic signs when evaluating a field's progress or a research program. They illustrate when concentration on one quality can harm long-term vitality.
